ext.description:
http://g.co/gtac
Slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/...

Alister Scott (Automattic)

Flaky tests are the bugbear of any automated test engineer; as someone (probably Alister) once said “insanity is running the same tests over and over again and getting different results”. Flaky tests cause no end of despair, but perhaps there’s no such thing as a flaky or non-flaky test, perhaps we need to look at this problem through a different lens. We should spend more time building more deterministic, more testable systems than spending time building resilient and persistent tests. Alister will share some examples of when test flakiness hid real problems underneath the system, and how it’s possible to solve test flakiness by building better systems.

How do you handle flaky tests in automation?

Answer: Flaky tests, which pass or fail inconsistently, are usually caused by timing issues, dynamic elements, or test dependencies. I stabilize flaky tests by:

Implementing explicit waits to ensure elements are interactable before performing actions.
Using retry mechanisms to re-run failed tests.
Isolating the environment to avoid dependencies on external systems.
Example: When testing a dynamic web element that loads with different IDs, I used a WebDriverWait to wait until the element was visible and ready for interaction, which stabilized the flaky tests.

content.text: Your Flaky Tests Are Burning $50K+ Per Year

ext.description: Every flaky test failure costs a developer 15-30 minutes. Multiply that by 5 failures a day and you're looking at 10-25 hours wasted per week. That's over $50,000 a year burned on tests that pass on retry.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​But the real cost isn't money — it's trust. When CI is flaky, developers stop checking. They merge without green checks. Real bugs slip through.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​I've seen teams where 70% of failures are just flakes.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​Quarantine them. Track your flake rate weekly.
